title: Sentence Structure
subtitle: Building the Sentence Castle
intro: Words are bricks; sentences are castles. Here Hana learns how to build sentences that stand strong: subjects and verbs that agree, clauses that connect, and no crumbling fragments or runaway run-ons.

rules.title: Subject + Predicate
rules.tagline: Every complete sentence needs a who and a does

story.line: Hana tries to build a wall. The bricks keep falling.
My sentence keeps collapsing! 'Ran through the forest.'
Who ran? A sentence needs two pillars. The subject is who or what. The predicate is what they do or are.
Kaito ran through the forest!
Now it stands. Kaito is the subject. 'Ran through the forest' is the predicate.
Why am I always the one running?

parts.name: Subject
parts.detail: Who or what the sentence is about. Usually a noun or pronoun.
parts.example: The old monk smiled.

parts.name: Predicate
parts.detail: The verb plus everything that tells about the subject.
parts.example: The old monk smiled at the children.

parts.name: Simple subject / verb
parts.detail: The core noun and core verb.
parts.example: monk / smiled

parts.name: Hidden subject
parts.detail: Commands have an invisible 'you.'
parts.example: (You) Sit down.

rules.history:
The idea of splitting a sentence into two halves comes from ancient Greek logic. Aristotle talked about a 'subject' (what you speak about) and a 'predicate' (what you say about it).

Grammarians borrowed his logic words, which is why grammar sounds a bit like philosophy class.

examples.good: The lanterns glowed.
Close the door.
examples.note: A command: the subject 'you' is understood.

examples.good: My best friend from school lives in Osaka.
examples.note: Subject: My best friend from school. Predicate: lives in Osaka.

rules.trick: Two pillars: WHO? and DOES WHAT? If either is missing, the castle falls.

quiz.q: What is the subject? 'The tired cat slept on the roof.'
quiz.why: The sentence is about the tired cat.
It has a subject (girl) and a verb (laughed).

rules.title: Word Order (S-V-O)

story.line: The dog bit the man. The man bit the dog. Same words, different story! Hehe.
Whoa. Just switching the order changes who bit who!
In English, word order does the work. Subject, Verb, Object. The doer comes first, the receiver comes after the verb.
In Japanese, the verb comes at the end! Kaito ramen eats.
Yes, Japanese is S-O-V and uses little markers like 'ga' and 'wo.' English lost most of its markers, so order must carry the meaning.

parts.name: S-V-O
parts.detail: Subject + Verb + Object.
parts.example: Hana (S) reads (V) manga (O).

parts.name: Adding places and times
parts.detail: Usually after the object: place, then time.
parts.example: She studied English at school yesterday.

parts.name: Indirect objects
parts.detail: Give someone something: S-V-IO-O or S-V-O-to-IO.
parts.example: He gave Yumi a gift. / He gave a gift to Yumi.

parts.name: Questions flip
parts.detail: The helper verb jumps before the subject.
parts.example: She is ready. → Is she ready?

rules.history:
Old English had case endings like German or Latin, so word order could be freer. 'Se hund bāt þone mann' and 'þone mann bāt se hund' both meant 'the dog bit the man,' because the endings marked who did what.

After 1066, those endings wore away, and English had to rely on position instead. By around 1400, S-V-O had become the standard order.

examples.good: I bought a new phone yesterday.
examples.bad: I bought yesterday a new phone.

examples.good: She speaks English very well.
examples.note: Don't put words between the verb and its object.

examples.good: We met our friends at the cafe.

rules.trick: Doer → Doing → Done-to. Then add Where, then When.

quiz.q: In 'The cat chased the mouse,' who did the chasing?

rules.title: Subject–Verb Agreement

story.line: The group of warriors are ready!
Find the true subject. Is it the warriors, or the group?
Of warriors is just a decoration. The real subject is group, and it's singular. 'The group of warriors IS ready.'
Excellent. Don't let words between the subject and verb trick you.
What about 'Neither Kaito nor his friends is ready'?
With or and nor, the verb agrees with the closer subject: neither Kaito nor his friends ARE ready.

parts.name: Basic rule
parts.detail: Singular subject → verb with -s (present). Plural subject → no -s.
parts.example: The dog barks. The dogs bark.

parts.name: Ignore the middle
parts.detail: Phrases between subject and verb don't count.
parts.example: The box of chocolates is on the table.

parts.name: And = plural
parts.detail: Two subjects joined by and.
parts.example: Hana and Kaito are friends.

parts.name: Or / nor = nearest
parts.detail: Match the closer subject.
parts.example: Either the cats or the dog is hungry.

parts.name: Each, every, everyone = singular
parts.detail: Even though they feel like many.
parts.example: Everyone is here.

rules.history:
Old English verbs matched their subjects with many different endings. Modern English has only one leftover in the present tense, the -s for he, she and it, plus the was/were split.

Because there's so little left, it's easy to slip. That's why agreement errors are among the most common mistakes even for native speakers.

examples.good: The list of names is long.
examples.bad: The list of names are long.

examples.good: Each of the students has a book.
examples.bad: Each of the students have a book.

examples.good: There are three cats outside.
examples.note: With there is / there are, the subject comes after the verb.

rules.trick: Cross out everything between the subject and the verb, then check if they match.

quiz.q: 'Neither the teacher nor the students ___ here.'
quiz.why: Students is closer to the verb, so plural.

rules.title: Simple, Compound & Complex
rules.tagline: Clauses: the rooms of the castle

story.line: A clause is a group of words with its own subject and verb. Think of it as a room in your castle.
One room: 'I trained.' That's a simple sentence.
Two equal rooms joined by a FANBOYS bridge: 'I trained, and Kaito slept.' Compound.
Hey! Okay: 'Because I was tired, I slept.'
That's complex: a main room (I slept) plus a dependent room (because I was tired) that can't stand alone.

parts.name: Independent clause
parts.detail: Can stand alone as a sentence.
parts.example: The rain stopped.

parts.name: Dependent clause
parts.detail: Starts with a word like because, when, if, although; cannot stand alone.
parts.example: when the rain stopped

parts.name: Simple sentence
parts.detail: One independent clause.
parts.example: The rain stopped.

parts.name: Compound sentence
parts.detail: Two independent clauses + comma + FANBOYS (or a semicolon).
parts.example: The rain stopped, so we went outside.

parts.name: Complex sentence
parts.detail: Independent + dependent clause.
parts.example: When the rain stopped, we went outside.

rules.history:
Latin and Greek teachers loved long, layered sentences. In the 1600s and 1700s, English writers imitated them, producing sentences that could fill a whole page.

Modern English style prefers mixing short and long sentences. Knowing the three types lets you control rhythm, like a director choosing fast cuts or slow scenes.

examples.good: I studied, but I failed the test.
Although I studied, I failed the test.
examples.note: Complex: although starts a dependent clause.

examples.good: If it rains, we'll stay home.
examples.note: Put a comma after a dependent clause that comes first.

rules.trick: Can it stand alone and make sense? It's an independent room. Does it start with because, if, when? It's a dependent room that needs a main room to lean on.

quiz.why: It has a dependent clause starting with after.
It starts with because and can't stand alone.

rules.title: Sentence Fragments
rules.tagline: Broken pieces that pretend to be sentences

story.line: Shards of a broken scroll lie on the floor.
'Because the dragon was hungry.' 'Running through the village.' 'The shiny red sword.'
Fragments. Each has a capital letter and a period, but something is missing: a subject, a verb, or a main clause.
Let me fix them! 'Because the dragon was hungry, it ate the crops.' 'The children were running through the village.' 'Kaito lost the shiny red sword.'
WHY is it always me?

parts.name: Missing subject
parts.detail: Who is doing it?
parts.example: Went to the store. → I went to the store.

parts.name: Missing verb
parts.detail: What happened?
parts.example: The big blue whale. → The big blue whale swam by.

parts.name: Lonely dependent clause
parts.detail: Attach it to an independent clause.
parts.example: Because I was late. → I ran because I was late.

parts.name: Style fragments
parts.detail: Writers sometimes use fragments on purpose for effect, especially in dialogue or ads.
parts.example: Silence. Then a scream.

rules.history:
Fragments are perfectly normal in speech. If someone asks 'Where are you going?' you answer 'Home.' Nobody says 'I am going home' every time.

In formal writing, teachers began strictly banning fragments in the 1800s as school grammar became standardized. Novelists and poets still break this rule on purpose for drama.

examples.good: We stayed inside because it was raining.
examples.bad: We stayed inside. Because it was raining.

examples.good: She left early to catch the train.
examples.bad: She left early. To catch the train.
examples.note: The second piece has no subject or main verb.

examples.good: Hana, a brave student, entered the cave.
examples.bad: Hana entered the cave. A brave student.

rules.trick: Read the piece alone, out loud, as if it's the first thing anyone ever said. If it leaves people asking 'What?', it's a fragment.

quiz.why: It's a dependent clause on its own.

quiz.q: Best fix for 'Walking to school in the snow.'
options: Walking to school, in the snow.
I was walking to school in the snow.
Walking. To school in the snow.
In the snow walking to school.
quiz.why: Adds a subject and a full verb.

rules.title: Run-ons & Comma Splices
rules.tagline: When sentences crash into each other

story.line: I woke up I ate breakfast I went to the dojo I trained all day I was tired!
Breathe, warrior, breathe.
That's a run-on: independent clauses smashed together with nothing between them.
Then I'll add commas! I woke up, I ate breakfast, I went to the dojo.
Now it's a comma splice. A comma alone is too weak to hold two sentences. Use a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus FANBOYS.

parts.name: Run-on (fused sentence)
parts.detail: Two clauses with no punctuation.
parts.example: It's late I'm going home.

parts.name: Comma splice
parts.detail: Two clauses joined by only a comma.
parts.example: It's late, I'm going home.

parts.name: Fix 1: period
parts.detail: Make two sentences.
parts.example: It's late. I'm going home.

parts.name: Fix 2: semicolon
parts.detail: Join closely related ideas.
parts.example: It's late; I'm going home.

parts.name: Fix 3: comma + FANBOYS, or because
parts.detail: Add a joining word.
parts.example: It's late, so I'm going home. / I'm going home because it's late.

rules.history:
Writers like Charles Dickens and Jane Austen sometimes used comma splices, especially in dialogue. In the 1800s and 1900s, school style guides made the rule much stricter.

Today comma splices are still common in casual messages, but in essays, exams and work emails, teachers and editors treat them as errors.

examples.good: I love ramen, but Yumi prefers sushi.
examples.bad: I love ramen, Yumi prefers sushi.

examples.good: The festival starts at six; don't be late.
examples.bad: The festival starts at six don't be late.

examples.good: She was tired. She went to bed.
examples.bad: She was tired she went to bed.

rules.trick: A comma is a little fence; it can't hold back two sentences. Use a wall (period), a gate (semicolon), or a fence plus a guard (comma + FANBOYS).

quiz.why: Two independent clauses with only a comma.

quiz.q: Which correctly fixes 'He was hungry he ate.'?
options: He was hungry, so he ate.
He was hungry so, he ate.

rules.title: Parallel Structure
rules.tagline: Keep lists and pairs in matching form

story.line: I like swimming, to hike, and riding bikes.
Your list is like a team where one member wears a different uniform.
Oh! Swimming, hiking, and riding bikes. All -ing!
Parallel structure. When items do the same job, give them the same grammatical form. It sounds balanced, like a drumbeat.
I came, I saw, I conquered!
Julius Caesar's famous parallel line. Short, matching, unforgettable.

parts.name: Lists
parts.detail: All nouns, all -ing, all to-verbs, all clauses.
parts.example: She likes reading, writing, and drawing.

parts.name: Pairs
parts.detail: Both sides of and/or/but should match.
parts.example: He is smart and kind. (not smart and has kindness)

parts.name: Correlative pairs
parts.detail: Either/or, not only/but also: match what follows each.
parts.example: Not only fast but also strong.

parts.name: Comparisons
parts.detail: Compare like with like.
parts.example: Swimming is harder than running. (not than to run)

rules.history:
Parallelism is one of the oldest tricks in rhetoric. Ancient Greek and Roman speakers trained in it, and Julius Caesar's 'Veni, vidi, vici' ('I came, I saw, I conquered,' 47 BC) is the classic example.

Later, famous speeches used it to be remembered: Abraham Lincoln's 'government of the people, by the people, for the people' (1863). Matching patterns are easier for brains to store.

examples.good: The job requires speed, accuracy, and patience.
examples.bad: The job requires speed, being accurate, and to be patient.

examples.good: She wants to travel and to learn.
examples.bad: She wants to travel and learning.

examples.good: He not only sings but also dances.
examples.bad: He not only sings but also is dancing.
examples.note: Match after each part of the pair.

rules.trick: Read only the first word of each list item. They should sound like the same kind of drumbeat: reading, writing, drawing.

options: I like to cook, bake, and eating.
I like cooking, baking, and eating.
I like to cook, baking, and eat.
I like cook, to bake, and eating.

quiz.q: Fix: 'She is talented, friendly, and works hard.'

rules.title: Misplaced & Dangling Modifiers
rules.tagline: Keep describing words next to what they describe

story.line: I read a sign today: 'Walking through the park, the trees were beautiful.'
Trees walking through the park? Like ents?!
A dangling modifier. The describing phrase has no correct person to attach to, so it grabs the nearest noun: the trees.
Fix: 'Walking through the park, I thought the trees were beautiful.'
I saw a dog in my pajamas!
Hehe. The dog was wearing your pajamas? That one's misplaced. 'In my pajamas, I saw a dog.'

parts.name: Modifier
parts.detail: A word or phrase that describes something.
parts.example: Covered in mud, the dog ran inside.

parts.name: Misplaced
parts.detail: The modifier is too far from what it describes.
parts.example: She served cake to the kids on paper plates.

parts.name: Dangling
parts.detail: The thing being described isn't in the sentence at all.
parts.example: After eating dinner, the dishes were washed.

parts.name: Fix
parts.detail: Put the doer right after the introductory phrase, or move the modifier.
parts.example: After eating dinner, we washed the dishes.

parts.name: Little word: only
parts.detail: Its position changes meaning.
parts.example: Only I ate cake. / I only ate cake. / I ate only cake.

rules.history:
Because English relies on word order (see S-V-O), a modifier attaches to whatever is closest. Languages with case endings can mark which word is described, but English can't.

Grammar books of the early 1900s collected funny dangling modifiers to teach this rule, and newspaper editors still trade them as jokes.

examples.good: Running late, I forgot my keys.
examples.bad: Running late, my keys were forgotten.
examples.note: Who was running late? I was.

examples.good: She ate almost the whole pizza.
examples.bad: She almost ate the whole pizza.
examples.note: If you mean she ate most of it, put almost next to whole. 'Almost ate' means she nearly ate it but didn't.

examples.good: Hana found a gold ring in the river.
examples.bad: Hana found a ring in the river that was gold.
examples.note: The river wasn't gold! Keep the description next to the ring.

rules.trick: The phrase at the start of a sentence describes the very next noun. Make sure that noun is the right one.

quiz.q: Which sentence has a dangling modifier?
options: I was tired, so I went to bed.
The bed looked inviting to me.

quiz.q: Fix: 'Having finished the test, the room was quiet.'
options: Having finished the test, the students sat quietly.
The room, having finished the test, was quiet.
Having finished the room, the test was quiet.
